headline: Japan's Trailblazing Mayor Shows Path Forward for Working Parents
meta_description: Shoko Kawata, Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave, has been named to TIME100 Next for challenging outdated assumptions about leadership and parenthood.
summary_short: Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave after giving birth has been recognized by TIME Magazine as one of the world's most influential rising leaders.
body:
Shoko Kawata, the 36-year-old mayor of Yawata City in Kyoto prefecture, has been named to TIME Magazine's TIME100 Next list—a recognition that arrives just weeks after she gave birth to her first child on 15 September. Her achievement marks a quiet but significant shift in a country grappling with historically low birth rates and rigid expectations about women in power. By taking maternity leave as an elected official, Kawata did something no Japanese mayor had done before, and in doing so, she sparked a national conversation about whether public service and parenthood can coexist.

The backlash was swift and unforgiving. Critics on social media called her decision "irresponsible" and argued she should resign. Some claimed that if she wanted children, she should never have taken office. Yet supporters saw something different: a woman refusing to choose between ambition and family, and in the process, opening doors for others. Kawata transferred her authority to deputy mayor Shigeto Nose for 16 weeks while arranging to work remotely when possible—a pragmatic solution born from necessity, since Japan's legal framework for elected officials lacks any maternity leave protections.

In an interview before giving birth, Kawata cut through the noise with clarity: "If we were to criticise politicians taking maternity leave, it means we are effectively excluding all women in their 20s through 40s from public office." After welcoming her daughter, she doubled down on her vision, posting that she wants to "reflect those experiences in real time into the policies I pursue"—transforming her personal choice into fuel for systemic change. Her TIME100 recognition suggests the world is watching to see if one mayor's courage can reshape what's possible.
